title: Remove K Digits
description: Brute force to optimized: k separate greedy scans versus a single monotonic non-decreasing stack pass applying the same greedy rule.

blocks.text: Given a non-negative integer num represented as a string, and an integer k, remove k digits from num so that the resulting number is the SMALLEST possible. Return the result as a string, with no leading zeros (unless the result is exactly "0").

blocks.caption: A monotonic non-decreasing stack greedily removes a "bigger digit before a smaller one," since that is always the digit safest to remove for minimizing the result

blocks.text: To make the resulting number as small as possible, more significant (earlier) digit positions matter more than less significant ones; whenever a digit is bigger than the digit immediately following it, removing that bigger, earlier digit always produces a result that is at least as small, making this greedy choice always safe.

blocks.title: Analogy: Editing a Multi-Digit Combination Lock to Be as Small as Possible
blocks.text: Imagine a combination lock with several dials, and being allowed to remove k dials entirely (shifting the remaining ones together) to make the resulting combination number as small as possible. Since earlier (more significant) dial positions matter far more than later ones, whenever a dial shows a BIGGER number than the dial right after it, removing that bigger, earlier dial is always the best choice, since it lets a smaller digit slide into that more significant position.

blocks.caption: Whenever the stack's top (most recently kept digit) is bigger than the incoming digit, and removals remain, popping it is always the greedy-optimal choice

blocks.text: Before removing one digit at a time using k SEPARATE scans (each looking for the single best digit to remove), notice that the SAME greedy rule (remove a bigger digit right before a smaller one) can be applied in a single continuous pass using a monotonic stack.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: To minimize the resulting number, the MOST significant digits matter the most, so whenever an earlier digit is bigger than a LATER one, removing the earlier (bigger) digit is always at least as good as keeping it.

Observation 2: This greedy rule can be applied REPEATEDLY as digits are processed left to right, using a stack of "kept so far" digits: each new digit gets a chance to "kick out" any bigger digits currently on top of the stack, as long as removals remain.

Observation 3: If the ENTIRE number turns out to already be non-decreasing (no digit is ever bigger than the one after it), the greedy rule never triggers, so any leftover removals must be taken from the very END of the number instead (removing the LEAST significant remaining digits does the least damage).

Observation 4: After the k removals are fully accounted for, any leading zeros in the result must be stripped (since numbers do not have leading zeros), with the special case that a fully-empty result defaults to "0".

This is a greedy monotonic stack technique: process digits left to right, popping a bigger "kept" digit whenever a smaller one arrives (as long as removals remain), then trimming any leftover removals from the end.

Remove exactly ONE digit at a time, k times: each time, find the first position where a digit is bigger than the one right after it (removing it), or if the number is fully non-decreasing, remove the very last digit.

items: Repeat k times: scan for the first digit that is bigger than its immediate next neighbor, and remove it; if no such digit exists, remove the very last digit instead.
After k removals, strip any leading zeros, defaulting to "0" if the result is empty.

codes.python:
def remove_k_digits(num, k):
    for _ in range(k):                                                     # remove ONE digit at a time, k times
        best_i = 0
        for i in range(1, len(num)):                                       # find the first digit that is bigger than its NEXT neighbor
            if num[i - 1] > num[i]:
                best_i = i - 1
                break
        else:
            best_i = len(num) - 1                                          # no such digit: num is non-decreasing, remove the LAST digit
        num = num[:best_i] + num[best_i + 1:]
    num = num.lstrip('0')
    return num if num else '0'


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(remove_k_digits("1432219", 3))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Each iteration directly applies the greedy rule (remove a bigger digit before a smaller one) exactly once, correctly finding the SINGLE best digit to remove at that step.
The fallback (remove the last digit) correctly handles a fully non-decreasing number, where no "bigger before smaller" pair exists.

blocks.text: Correctly applies the greedy removal rule k times, producing the smallest possible result, since each individual removal is provably optimal given the remaining digits.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(k*n), since each of the k removals requires an O(n) scan (plus an O(n) string rebuild).
Space: O(n), for the string being repeatedly modified.
Limitation: repeating a full scan for EACH of the k removals is wasteful; a single monotonic stack pass applies the identical greedy rule to ALL digits at once, needing only one linear scan total.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rescans the entire string for every single removal. Instead, process digits left to right using a stack of "kept" digits: for each new digit, while removals remain AND the stack's top digit is bigger than the new digit, pop it (removing that bigger digit). Push the new digit. If removals still remain after processing the whole string (a fully non-decreasing number), trim them from the END of the stack.

Walk through num with a stack. For each digit c: while k > 0 and the stack is non-empty and its top is > c, pop and decrement k. Push c. After the full walk, if k > 0, pop k more digits from the end. Join the stack, strip leading zeros, defaulting to "0" if empty.
Use a monotonic non-decreasing stack, greedily popping a bigger "kept" digit whenever a smaller one arrives, in a single linear pass.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The stack is "1219" (k already fully used, no trailing removal needed), matching the expected result.

codes.python:
def remove_k_digits(num, k):
    stack = []                                                              # a monotonic NON-DECREASING stack of "kept" digits
    for c in num:
        while k > 0 and stack and stack[-1] > c:                           # a bigger digit right before a smaller one: always safe to remove
            stack.pop()
            k -= 1
        stack.append(c)

    while k > 0:                                                            # if removals remain (num was fully non-decreasing), trim from the END
        stack.pop()
        k -= 1

    result = ''.join(stack).lstrip('0')                                    # strip any leading zeros
    return result if result else '0'


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(remove_k_digits("1432219", 3))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single linear pass (each digit is pushed once and popped at most once).
Space: O(n), for the stack.

The greedy rule (remove a bigger digit right before a smaller one) is provably optimal for minimizing the resulting number: swapping a bigger EARLIER digit for a smaller LATER one at the same position always produces a smaller or equal result, since more significant digit positions dominate the comparison. Applying this rule continuously via a stack (instead of repeatedly rescanning) achieves the identical optimal result in a single pass, since each pop represents exactly one greedy removal, and the loop naturally stops once k removals are used up.

items: The while loop's three conditions (k > 0, stack non-empty, top > current digit) must ALL hold for a pop to be safe and meaningful.
The final "trim from the end if k remains" step correctly handles a fully (or partially) non-decreasing number, where the greedy rule never fully exhausts k during the main pass.
Stripping leading zeros AFTER all removals are applied correctly handles cases like num = "10200", k = 1, which would otherwise leave a leading zero in the raw stack result.

blocks.text: Minimizing a number by removing digits is a greedy monotonic-stack problem: a bigger digit immediately before a smaller one is always safe to remove, and applying this rule via a stack in a single pass (rather than repeatedly rescanning) achieves the optimal result efficiently.

items: Forgetting the "removals remain" (k > 0) check in the popping condition, which could remove more digits than allowed.
Forgetting to trim leftover removals from the END when the number turns out to be fully (or partially) non-decreasing.
Forgetting to strip leading zeros from the final result, or mishandling the special case where the result is completely empty (defaulting to "0").

items: Explicitly proving (or at least clearly stating) WHY "remove a bigger digit before a smaller one" is always safe (more significant positions dominate the comparison) demonstrates a rigorous understanding of the greedy choice, not just a memorized rule.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Remove k digits/characters to make the result the SMALLEST (or LARGEST) possible" points toward a greedy monotonic stack, removing digits that violate the desired monotonic order.

items: How would this change if the goal were to make the resulting number the LARGEST possible instead? Use a monotonic DECREASING stack instead (pop a SMALLER digit before a bigger one), the mirror-image greedy rule.

Why is the trailing removal step (after the main pass) needed, and when does it actually trigger? It handles the case where num is fully (or partially) non-decreasing, meaning the greedy rule never finds enough "bigger before smaller" pairs to use up all k removals during the main scan.

How would you formally prove the greedy choice is optimal? An exchange argument: for any two candidate results that differ at their first differing position, whichever one has the smaller digit AT that position is unconditionally smaller overall, regardless of what follows.

A greedy variant of the monotonic stack pattern, related to Next Greater Element I and Daily Temperatures elsewhere in this category, but here driven by a REMOVAL-COUNT-LIMITED greedy choice rather than a simple next-match search.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(k*n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (monotonic non-decreasing stack, one pass): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Greedy monotonic non-decreasing stack

Core Idea: A bigger "kept" digit right before a smaller incoming digit is always safe to remove (more significant positions dominate); apply this via a stack in one pass, then trim any leftover removals from the end
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: If the number is fully non-decreasing, the greedy rule never triggers, so leftover removals must come from the very END instead
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Pop a bigger top while k>0 and top>current; push current; trim k more from the end if needed; strip leading zeros
